USMLE-style practice · Pathology

Identifying an extracellular lesion

Choose the single best answer, then reveal the explanation.

A pathologist examines a renal biopsy from a patient with progressive proteinuria. Pale eosinophilic material expands the mesangium and vessel walls. Electron microscopy shows randomly arranged nonbranching fibrils, and Congo red is positive. Where is the pathogenic material principally located?

  1. Outside cells in the extracellular matrix
  2. Within hepatocyte lipid droplets
  3. Within lysosomal residual bodies only
  4. Within plasma-cell rough endoplasmic reticulum only
  5. Within erythrocyte nuclei
Reveal answer and explanation
Correct answer

Outside cells in the extracellular matrix

Amyloid is an extracellular protein deposit; its location distinguishes it from intracellular storage inclusions.

Understanding the options

Outside cells in the extracellular matrix
Amyloid is an extracellular protein deposit; its location distinguishes it from intracellular storage inclusions.
Within hepatocyte lipid droplets
This describes steatosis and does not explain glomerular fibrils.
Within lysosomal residual bodies only
Residual bodies contain incompletely degraded intracellular material.
Within plasma-cell rough endoplasmic reticulum only
Immunoglobulin retention can form Russell bodies, which are intracellular.
Within erythrocyte nuclei
Mature erythrocytes lack nuclei and cannot contain these extracellular deposits.
